seoTitle: How to Create a Scheduled Flow in Power Automate
metaDescription: Build a scheduled cloud flow in Power Automate: pick the scheduled flow type, configure the Recurrence trigger's start time and frequency, add actions, and confirm it runs.
intro: A scheduled flow is Power Automate's answer to anything that needs to happen on a timer instead of in response to an event: a weekly report, a nightly backup, a recurring reminder. The setup takes a handful of screens: choosing the scheduled flow type, configuring the Recurrence trigger, adding the actions it performs, and confirming a run actually succeeded. This guide follows a real example flow called Weekly Project Report from creation through its first successful test run.
costNote: Scheduled flows don't need a Power Automate Premium license on their own; a Microsoft 365 license covers them as long as every connector the flow uses is a standard connector, per Microsoft's licensing FAQ. The moment one action in the flow uses a premium connector, the flow's owner needs a Premium (or Process) license, regardless of who else the flow is shared with.

steps.heading: Choose Scheduled cloud flow when creating a flow
steps.body: From My flows, select New flow, or from the Create page, you're offered several starting points: Automated cloud flow, Instant cloud flow, Scheduled cloud flow, Describe it to design it (Copilot), Desktop flow, and Process mining. Scheduled cloud flow is built specifically for time-based automation, its subtitle reads "You choose when and how often it runs", which separates it from Automated (triggered by an event) or Instant (triggered manually). If you have Copilot access, you can also describe the schedule in plain language instead of building it screen by screen; this guide follows the manual path. Community templates below the blank-start options, things like "Schedule a reply to send at the perfect time", are worth a scan in case one already does most of what you need.

image.caption: The flow creation screen showing the six starting options, with Scheduled cloud flow highlighted as the one for time-based automation.

steps.heading: Set the starting time and repeat interval
steps.body: Naming your flow and picking Scheduled cloud flow asks for two things upfront: a Starting date and time, and how often to Repeat every (an interval in minutes, hours, days, weeks, or months). Confirming these drops you into the designer canvas with a single Recurrence block sitting at the top. For anything more specific than a plain interval, a particular time of day, particular days of the week, open the Recurrence trigger and select Show advanced options; that's where Time zone, At these hours, At these minutes, and, for a weekly schedule, On these days actually live. Everything else in the flow builds downward from this block using the plus icon underneath it.

image.caption: A fresh scheduled flow canvas with just the Recurrence trigger placed, ready for actions to be added below it.

steps.heading: Add the actions the flow should perform
steps.body: Click the plus icon below Recurrence to add your first action. In the example flow, that's Get file metadata, connected to OneDrive for Business; the parameters panel on the left lets you browse folders to pick the exact file the flow should check each run. This is the pattern for every action you add: configure its connection, point it at the right file or data source, and let it feed into whatever comes next, whether that's generating a report, sending an email, or writing to another system. Worth noting for licensing: most file and email connectors are standard, but if an action you add is a premium connector, the flow's owner will need a Premium or Process license to keep it running.

image.caption: The Get file metadata action added under Recurrence, with a OneDrive for Business folder picker open to select the target file.

steps.heading: Save the flow and give it a clear name
steps.body: Power Automate saves flows under the name given at creation, "Weekly Project Report" in this walkthrough, and that name shows up in My flows, in run history, and in any notifications tied to it. Pick something that describes what the flow does and how often, not a generic placeholder; you'll be scanning a list of flow names later when something needs troubleshooting, and a vague name won't help.

steps.heading: Test the flow and confirm it ran
steps.body: Once saved, open the flow's details page to see its Status (On), Type (Scheduled), owner, connections, and a 28-day run history table listing every execution with its start time, duration, and status. In the example, a manual test run completed in a few seconds and shows "Test succeeded" in the Status column, confirmation the flow is wired correctly before it runs unattended on its own schedule. This page is also where a failure shows up early: a red "Failed" status means fixing the flow now, not waiting for someone to notice a report never arrived.

image.caption: The Weekly Project Report flow's details page, showing its Scheduled type, On status, connections, and a run history entry marked Test succeeded.

steps.heading: Monitor it going forward
steps.body: After the first successful run, check the run history periodically rather than assuming a scheduled flow will quietly work forever; connections can expire, source files can move, and permissions can change. The same details page used to confirm the test run is where every future execution logs its status, so bookmarking it, or checking My flows regularly, is enough to catch problems before they turn into a pattern of missed reports.

faq.question: How often can a scheduled flow run?
faq.answer: The Recurrence trigger accepts an interval in minutes, hours, days, weeks, or months, with additional day/time controls under Show advanced options for daily and weekly patterns.

faq.question: Does a scheduled flow cost extra on top of Microsoft 365?
faq.answer: Not by itself. A scheduled flow built entirely from standard connectors runs under a Microsoft 365 license. It only needs a Power Automate Premium (or Process) license if one of its actions uses a premium connector.

faq.question: Can I change the schedule after creating the flow?
faq.answer: Yes. Open the flow in the designer, select the Recurrence trigger, adjust its interval, start time, or advanced day/time options, then save; downstream actions aren't affected.

faq.question: How do I check if a scheduled flow ran successfully?
faq.answer: Open the flow's details page and check the run history table, which lists each execution's start time, duration, and status, such as "Test succeeded" or a failure state.

faq.question: What's the difference between Scheduled and Automated cloud flows?
faq.answer: A Scheduled cloud flow runs on a recurrence you define. An Automated cloud flow is triggered by an event instead, like a new email arriving or a file being created.
